Both futurists and preterists quote the early church writers. Some futurists argue that writers only a generation or two from the apostles must have known the truth. The fulfilled reading accepts that history is useful. But it says the Bible alone is the rule of faith. Godly teachers have often been wrong about prophecy. Even in the apostles' day some believers misread Jesus' words (John 21:22-23). The Bereans checked even Paul against Scripture (Acts 17:11). Paul warned against traditions of men (Colossians 2:8). Read this way, the fathers show how early Christians read prophecy. But their views must be tested by the text. A long list of names can never override what the Bible states plainly.
John 21:22-23: a saying spread among believers that John would not die, but Jesus never said that.
Acts 17:11: the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to test Paul's teaching.

Most Protestants of every view agree that Scripture alone is the final authority. Futurists still value the fathers as early witnesses to how the apostles' teaching was understood. Catholic and Orthodox Christians give a larger role to tradition, while still seeing it as faithful to Scripture.
Did the early church writers link the beast or antichrist to Nero or Rome?
Several did. Some linked the beast's number to "Lateinos" (Latin), and Victorinus and others saw Nero in Revelation 17. Others expected a future antichrist.

A futurist pastor once asked: if Nero was the beast, why did the fathers not say so? The fulfilled reading answers that some did connect the beast with Rome or Nero. Irenaeus suggested that 666 might spell "Lateinos", meaning a Latin or Roman (Against Heresies 5.30.3). Victorinus, about AD 300, saw Nero as one of the kings in Revelation 17. Tertullian said Nero was the first to stain the rising faith with blood (Scorpiace 15). Augustine reported that many believed Nero would rise again as antichrist (City of God 20.19). Fairness requires adding that most of these writers still expected an antichrist in the future. They mixed past and future. Read this way, the fathers do not give a clear futurist witness either.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3: "Lateinos" in Greek letters adds up to 666.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero's cruel punishment of Christians after the fire of Rome in AD 64.

Futurists point out that Irenaeus clearly expected a future antichrist who would rebuild the temple and reign three and a half years (Against Heresies 5.25.4; 5.30.4). They note that he placed John's vision in Domitian's reign (5.30.3). They argue that the fathers saw Nero, at most, as a type of a later antichrist.
Are writers close to the apostles' time always reliable on prophecy?
No. Nearness in time does not guarantee accuracy. Irenaeus, for example, also wrote that Jesus lived to nearly fifty, which almost no one accepts.

One futurist argument says the fathers' own fathers and grandfathers would have told them about the antichrist. The fulfilled reading answers that second- and third-hand reports can be wrong. Irenaeus, a strong early witness, claimed that Jesus was nearly fifty when he died (Against Heresies 2.22.5). He also passed on a saying, from Papias, about vines with ten thousand branches in the coming kingdom (Against Heresies 5.33.3). Few accept these today. Popular myths spread even in modern times. Many people still believe medieval scholars thought the earth was flat. Historians have shown that educated people knew it was round. Read this way, the plain words of Scripture, written by eyewitnesses, outweigh later reports. "This generation" (Matthew 24:34) is firmer ground than tradition.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5: Jesus said to be past forty, against Luke 3:23.
Jeffrey Burton Russell, Inventing the Flat Earth (1991), shows the flat-earth belief was a later myth.

Futurists agree that the fathers made mistakes. But they say a broad and early agreement, such as early belief in a future antichrist and a millennium, carries weight. Historians of all views use the fathers carefully, testing each claim and weighing early, multiple witnesses above single reports.
Did the early fathers believe in an "any moment" rapture?
No. Scholars on several sides agree they expected antichrist, tribulation and Christ's return soon, in that order. That is not the modern idea of a secret, any-moment rapture.

Dispensational writers sometimes quote the fathers' hope for Christ's coming as support for an any-moment rapture. George Eldon Ladd, a historic premillennialist, studied the evidence. He found that the early church expected the whole cluster of events to come soon: antichrist, tribulation and then Christ. That is not the same as a coming that could happen before any sign. A 1977 Dallas Seminary thesis by a dispensational writer reached a similar result. It found that the early fathers held to the immediacy of Christ's return, but not to a pretribulation rapture. On the fulfilled reading, the fathers show that early Christians took the time words as "soon". But they applied them to their own day, after AD 70, and so misapplied them.
Didache 16: believers must watch, for false prophets and the world-deceiver will appear before the Lord comes.
Shepherd of Hermas, Vision 2.2.7: blessed are those who endure the great tribulation that is coming.

Pretribulationists say the early church's expectancy shows a seed of the any-moment view, even if not fully developed. Some cite Pseudo-Ephraem, a text from roughly the 4th to 7th century, as an early rapture witness, though its meaning is disputed. Posttribulationists agree with Ladd that the fathers expected to face antichrist.
Can an "imminent" event also be called "soon"?
One pretribulational writer said no: if an event is "soon", it must happen within a short time. The fulfilled reading uses this to say "near" and "soon" must mean what they say.

Renald Showers, a defender of the any-moment rapture, wrote that a person cannot properly say an imminent event will happen soon. "Soon" means within a short time after a set point. He meant that imminent events may or may not be soon. On the fulfilled reading, this is a revealing admission. If "soon" means within a short time, then the Bible's own words, "soon", "near" and "at hand", place the events within a short time of their writing. The texts do not say the coming is "imminent" in Showers's sense. They say it is "near" (Revelation 1:3) and that it will "shortly" happen (Revelation 22:6). Read this way, the definition of "soon" offered by a futurist supports the fulfilled reading.
Revelation 1:3 and 22:10: "the time is near" frames the whole book.
Romans 13:11-12: "the night is far spent, the day is at hand" (KJV).

Pretribulationists answer that the Bible teaches both: the Lord is near, and his coming is sudden and unknown in date (Matthew 24:44). They say both are true from God's point of view. Amillennialists say "near" describes the whole last days between Christ's two comings.
Did Ignatius and Cyprian think they lived in the last times, and were they right?
Yes, they thought so. The fulfilled reading says they misapplied texts meant for the apostles' generation. Paul said the ends of the ages had come upon his own readers.

About AD 107, Ignatius of Antioch wrote, "These are the last times" (Ephesians 11). In the 250s, Cyprian of Carthage wrote that the end of the world and the time of antichrist were drawing near. He urged believers to prepare for battle. He saw the persecution of his day as the great trial. On the fulfilled reading, both men were sincere, but both were wrong to apply the time texts to their own day. Paul had already told the Corinthians that "the ends of the ages" had come upon them (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews said Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26). Read this way, the last days were the last days of the old covenant era. Later Christians who claimed them for their own times repeated a mistake.
1 Corinthians 10:11: "upon whom the ends of the world are come" (KJV).
Cyprian, Epistle 55 (ANF numbering): the time of antichrist draws near.

Amillennialists say Ignatius and Cyprian were right in a sense, because the whole church age is "the last times". Futurists say every generation should live expecting the end. Both reject the idea that the last days ended in AD 70, while agreeing that Cyprian and others misjudged the date.
Did Justin Martyr apply Matthew 24 to his own day?
Yes. He said Jesus' warning about false prophets and false Christs was being fulfilled before his eyes, and he expected antichrist soon.

Justin wrote his Dialogue with Trypho about AD 155-160. He quoted Jesus' warnings that many false Christs and false prophets would arise (Matthew 24:11). He said Christians saw these things fulfilled in his time, in the heresies around them (Dialogue 35). He also expected the man of apostasy to come soon (Dialogue 110). On the fulfilled reading, Justin shows how early writers read the Olivet Discourse as speaking to their own day. They did not read it as an any-moment rapture or a distant future. But he too stretched texts that Jesus tied to his own generation. Read this way, Justin is a witness that "near" was taken as near. But his own application was mistaken.
Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 35: Christians see Jesus' predictions of false teachers being fulfilled.
Matthew 24:11, 24: false prophets and false Christs would deceive many.

Many interpreters note that false teachers arise in every age, so Justin was not wrong to see a pattern. Futurists cite Justin as an early premillennialist who expected Christ's thousand-year reign in Jerusalem (Dialogue 80-81). Amillennialists note that Justin admitted many true Christians did not share his millennial view.
What does the early account of James's death show about the expected coming?
Hegesippus records James saying Jesus was "about to come on the clouds of heaven". He adds that Vespasian's invasion followed soon after.

Hegesippus, a second-century Christian writer, is quoted by Eusebius (Church History 2.23). He says James, the brother of Jesus, was asked about Jesus by temple leaders. James replied that the Son of Man sits at the right hand of the great Power and "is about to come" on the clouds of heaven. This echoes Jesus' words at his trial (Matthew 26:64). James was thrown from the temple and killed. Josephus dates James's death to AD 62 (Antiquities 20.9.1). Hegesippus says that immediately after this, Vespasian invaded Judea. On the fulfilled reading, the account links Jesus' coming on the clouds with the judgment on Jerusalem. Read this way, a witness from Jesus' own family expected it soon.
Matthew 26:64: Jesus told the high priest, "you shall see" the Son of Man coming on the clouds.
AD 62: Josephus (Antiquities 20.9.1) records James's execution by the high priest Ananus.

Other readers say James spoke of Christ's final coming, and that Hegesippus later linked the war to James's death as a judgment. Scholars debate how accurate Hegesippus's account is, since it differs from Josephus in details. Futurists see the account as proof of early expectation, not of fulfilment.
Did John himself point to a near fulfilment of Revelation (Revelation 1:19)?
The 19th-century scholar F. W. Farrar thought so. He saw "the things which are, and the things which are about to happen" as a sign of near events.

Frederic Farrar argued that the true founder of the preterist reading was John himself. Revelation 1:19 tells John to write what he saw, "the things which are", and the things "which are about to" happen after these. The Greek verb mello often means "about to". Farrar said John's repeated themes were speed ("en tachei") and nearness ("the time is near"). He said language is meaningless if every commentator can stretch "speedily" and "near" into many centuries. On the fulfilled reading, this shows that some respected scholars outside the movement saw the same point. Read this way, the time words of Revelation frame the whole book. They mark it as a message about events that were then on the horizon.
Revelation 1:19: "the things which shall be hereafter" (KJV), where the Greek has "are about to".
F. W. Farrar, The Early Days of Christianity (1882), Dean of Canterbury from 1895.

Futurists divide Revelation by 1:19 into past (ch. 1), present (chs. 2-3) and future (chs. 4-22). They read mello as "will", not "about to". Idealists see "the things which are" as the ongoing battle between the church and the world in every age.
Did the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament expect Christ to come soon?
Yes. 1 Clement, the Didache, Barnabas and Ignatius all urged readiness for a coming they expected soon. The fulfilled reading says they misapplied texts written for the apostles' generation.

1 Clement, written about AD 96, says God's will shall be done "soon and suddenly". It cites Isaiah and Malachi (1 Clement 23). The Didache, perhaps late first century, warns readers to watch because the Lord is coming (Didache 16). The Epistle of Barnabas says the day is near when all things will perish (Barnabas 21). Ignatius tells Polycarp to await the one who is above time (Polycarp 3). One dispensational scholar who studied these writers concluded that they believed in the immediacy of the second coming. On the fulfilled reading, if these writers expected Jesus in their day after AD 70, they were mistaken. That does not make the Bible mistaken. Read this way, the Bible's "soon" belonged to the apostolic generation.
1 Clement 23 quotes Malachi 3:1: "the Lord shall suddenly come to his temple".
Didache 16.1: "Watch over your life ... for you do not know the hour" (paraphrase).

Futurists see these writings as early evidence of an expectant church, which they share. Amillennialists say watchfulness is right in every age. Critical scholars see the delay of the coming as a problem the early church slowly adjusted to. Most agree the fathers did not hold a pretribulation rapture.
Why did readings of prophecy change after the fourth century?
When persecution ended under Constantine, many Christians stopped expecting the end soon. Spiritual readings became dominant. Modern futurism came much later, after 1590.

Early writers often saw Roman persecution as the great tribulation and the emperor as antichrist. In AD 313 the Edict of Milan gave Christians legal freedom under Constantine. Hope for an earthly millennium declined. Tyconius and Augustine read Revelation as a picture of the church's struggle in every age (City of God 20). The fulfilled reading says that over time, many interpreters relativised the time words. History needs a correction here. The main view after Augustine was not modern futurism. Systematic futurism began with the Jesuit Francisco Ribera about 1590. It spread among Protestants through John Nelson Darby and the Scofield Bible in the 1800s and 1900s. On the fulfilled reading, each new system reinterpreted the time texts instead of letting them stand.
AD 313: the Edict of Milan ended the legal persecution of Christians.
About 1590: Francisco Ribera's commentary placed most of Revelation in a future three and a half years.

Amillennialists see Augustine's shift as a sound reading of Revelation 20, not a reaction to politics. Futurists trace their views to early premillennialists such as Irenaeus and Justin, not only to Ribera and Darby. Historicists, dominant among Protestants from the Reformation to the 1800s, read Revelation as church history.
Can we be sure what "the fathers" believed about prophecy?
Only in part. Their writings are vast, much is untranslated, and they disagreed with each other. Claims about "what the fathers taught" should be made with care.

The Latin and Greek collections of early Christian writers edited by J.-P. Migne in the 19th century fill over 380 large volumes. Much of this remains untranslated into English. The fathers also disagreed. Some were premillennial, like Justin and Irenaeus. Others, like Origen and later Augustine, were not. Their guesses about the antichrist varied widely. Historians of prophetic interpretation show little agreement, across the centuries, on who the antichrist is. On the fulfilled reading, this is another reason to rest on Scripture alone. If the fathers did not agree, they cannot settle the debate. Read this way, the only fixed standard is the inspired text and its own time words.
Patrologia Latina (217 volumes plus indexes) and Patrologia Graeca (161 volumes): Migne's collections.
Justin admitted that many "of pure and pious faith" did not hold his millennial view (Dialogue 80).

Historians on all sides agree the fathers were diverse. Futurists still find a clear early strand of premillennial and future-antichrist teaching. Preterists find early hints of past fulfilment, such as Eusebius on AD 70 (Church History 3.5-8). Each side should present the evidence fairly and fully.
Does Zechariah 14 describe Christ's second coming and a thousand-year reign?
Premillennialists say yes. The fulfilled reading says the chapter follows the striking of the Shepherd (13:7) and describes the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 and the rise of Christ's kingdom.

Many premillennialists read Zechariah 14 as the end of the age. The nations attack Jerusalem, Christ descends to the Mount of Olives, and he begins a millennial reign. The fulfilled reading begins with the chapter's setting. Zechariah 13:7 says the Shepherd will be struck and the sheep scattered. Jesus applied this to his own arrest (Mark 14:27). What follows, on this reading, belongs to the same era. There is the refining of a remnant (13:8-9), the capture of Jerusalem (14:2) and the Lord's victory (14:3). Jesus' parable says the king "sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city" (Matthew 22:7). Read this way, the chapter fits the first century. It does not leap over AD 70 to a distant future.
Mark 14:27: "I will smite the shepherd" (KJV), quoted from Zechariah 13:7.
Matthew 22:7: the king sends armies and burns the city of those who refused the wedding.

Premillennialists note that Zechariah 14 ends with the LORD as king over all the earth and nations keeping the Feast of Tabernacles (14:9, 16). They see this as a future earthly kingdom. Amillennialists often read the chapter as symbolic of the whole church age, ending in the final judgment.
Who are "all the nations" gathered against Jerusalem in Zechariah 14:2?
On the fulfilled reading, they are the Roman armies of AD 66-70. Rome's forces included soldiers and allied kings drawn from many nations.

Zechariah 14:2 says God will gather all nations against Jerusalem. The city is taken, houses plundered, and half the city goes into exile. On the fulfilled reading, this fits Rome's war. The Roman Empire ruled most of the known world (Luke 2:1). Its armies included legions and auxiliary troops recruited across the empire. Josephus also lists allied kings who sent forces to Titus, such as Agrippa II, Antiochus of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa and Malchus of Arabia (Jewish War 3.4.2). God had used Assyria as the rod of his anger in the same way (Isaiah 10:5-6). Older commentators such as Thomas Scott read Zechariah 14:2 this way. Read this way, Rome's multinational army fulfilled "all nations".
Josephus, Jewish War 3.4.2: allied kings sent infantry and cavalry to the Roman army.
Luke 2:1: Caesar's decree to enroll "all the world", meaning the Roman world.

Futurists say "all nations" means a future world coalition against Israel, matching Zechariah 12:3 and Revelation 16:14-16. They note that in Zechariah 14 the LORD rescues Jerusalem by fighting the nations, which did not happen in AD 70. Amillennialists often see a symbolic picture of the world against God's people.
What do "half the city into exile" and "the rest not cut off" mean (Zechariah 14:2)?
On the fulfilled reading, many were killed or enslaved in AD 70, while a remnant was spared. Some read "not cut off" as the Jewish believers who joined the heavenly Jerusalem.

Zechariah 14:2 says half the city will go into exile, but the rest of the people will not be cut off from the city. In AD 70, Josephus says 97,000 captives were taken and many sent to mines or arenas (Jewish War 6.9.2-3). Before the siege, the Jerusalem church fled to Pella, as Jesus warned (Matthew 24:16). Eusebius reports this (Church History 3.5.3). The commentator Thomas Scott suggested that those who believed became citizens of "the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:22). So they were "not cut off" from the true city of God. Read this way, Zechariah 14:2 describes both judgment and a preserved remnant. This is the same pattern Paul saw in his own day (Romans 11:5).
Josephus, Jewish War 6.9.3: 97,000 taken captive during the war.
Hebrews 12:22: believers "are come unto mount Sion ... the heavenly Jerusalem" (KJV).

Futurists read this as a future siege in which half of Jerusalem is captured before the LORD intervenes. They note that the remnant remains in the city itself. Amillennialists may see a picture of the church preserved through trouble.
When did the LORD "fight against those nations" (Zechariah 14:3)?
On the fulfilled reading, God first used Rome to judge Jerusalem, then judged Rome itself, as he did Assyria. Its fall came over the following centuries.

Zechariah 14:3 says the LORD will go out and fight against the nations. The fulfilled reading sees a pattern from Isaiah. God sent Assyria against his people, then punished Assyria's pride (Isaiah 10:5-12). In the same way, Rome destroyed Jerusalem, then faced God's judgment. Some older commentators wrote that Rome never prospered as before. The facts need care here. Rome went through civil war in AD 68-69, the "year of four emperors". But the empire then grew, reaching its largest size under Trajan in AD 117. Its long decline came in the third to fifth centuries. Read this way, God's judgment on Rome was real but gradual. The stone of Daniel 2 slowly crushed the empire as Christ's kingdom grew (Daniel 2:34-35, 44).
AD 68-69: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian ruled in quick succession amid civil war (Tacitus, Histories 1.2).
Isaiah 10:12: after using Assyria, God punishes the Assyrian king's pride.

Futurists say Zechariah 14:3 describes Christ's personal return to destroy armies gathered at Jerusalem (Revelation 19:11-21). They note that in AD 70 God did not defend Jerusalem, while in Zechariah 14 he does. Amillennialists may see the final judgment of all God's enemies.
Must "his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives" mean a bodily descent of Christ?
Futurists say yes, linking it to Acts 1:11. The fulfilled reading notes that the prophets often describe God "coming down" in judgment without a bodily visit.

Zechariah 14:4 says that on that day the LORD's feet will stand on the Mount of Olives. The fulfilled reading points out that the verse does not say he comes down from heaven. Elsewhere, the Old Testament often speaks of God coming down. He "came down" to deliver Israel from Egypt (Exodus 3:8). He came down on Mount Sinai (Nehemiah 9:13). David prayed, "Bow your heavens and come down; touch the mountains" (Psalms 144:5). Micah said the LORD would come and tread on the high places, and the mountains would melt (Micah 1:3-4). In none of these did God appear in a body. Read this way, Zechariah 14:4 uses the same picture of God acting in judgment near Jerusalem. Jesus gave his discourse on Jerusalem's fall from that very mountain (Matthew 24:3).
Micah 1:3-4: the LORD comes down, and valleys split like wax before fire.
Isaiah 31:4: the LORD "comes down" to fight for Mount Zion.

Futurists point to Acts 1:11-12. Jesus ascended from the Mount of Olives, and the angels said he would return "in like manner". They see a clear link with Zechariah 14:4. Many amillennialists also link the two texts to the final return, though they read the land changes symbolically.
What do mountains symbolize in prophecy?
Often kingdoms or powers. Babylon is a "destroying mountain", and God's kingdom is a stone that becomes a great mountain. The fulfilled reading reads Zechariah 14 with this in mind.

Prophets often use mountains as symbols. Isaiah says the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised above all mountains, and nations will stream to it (Isaiah 2:2). God calls Babylon a "destroying mountain" that he will burn (Jeremiah 51:25). In Daniel's vision a stone becomes a great mountain that fills the earth (Daniel 2:35). Daniel explains that it is the kingdom God sets up (Daniel 2:44). Revelation is full of Old Testament imagery and uses mountains in the same way (Revelation 8:8; Revelation 17:9). On the fulfilled reading, the Mount of Olives splitting is not mainly about geology. It is about a change in kingdoms. The old order centred on Jerusalem gives way to Christ's worldwide kingdom.
Jeremiah 51:25: Babylon, a "destroying mountain", becomes "a burnt mountain".
Daniel 2:35, 44: the stone becomes a mountain, which is God's everlasting kingdom.

Futurists agree that mountains can be symbols. But they hold that Zechariah 14:4 names a real place, east of Jerusalem, and expect a real earthquake. They note that Zechariah 14:5 compares it with the earthquake in King Uzziah's days (Amos 1:1). Amillennialists read the change as spiritual and final.
Is the prophets' language about leveled hills and split mountains meant literally?
Often not. Isaiah 40:4 promised that every mountain would be made low, and Luke 3:5 applies it to John the Baptist's ministry, with no change to Judea's hills.

Isaiah 40:3-4 says to prepare the way of the LORD. Every valley will be raised and every mountain and hill made low. Luke applies this to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus (Luke 3:4-6). No hills in Judea were levelled. Yet the prophecy was fulfilled in the first century. On the fulfilled reading, this gives a key for Zechariah 14. Prophets often describe God's acts with pictures of shaking land. Mountains skip (Psalms 114:4). Hills bow down (Habakkuk 3:6). Trees clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12). These are real events told in poetic form. Read this way, the Mount of Olives splitting describes a great change in God's dealings. It is not mainly a forecast of land movement.
Luke 3:4-6: Isaiah 40:3-5 is fulfilled as John prepares the way, with no change to the land.
Isaiah 55:12: "all the trees of the field shall clap their hands" (KJV).

Futurists agree that poetry is common, but say Zechariah 14 is detailed narrative prophecy. It gives directions (east-west, north-south), a valley reaching to Azel, and a comparison with a real earthquake. They expect a literal fulfilment, possibly along known fault lines. Amillennialists read the details as a picture of final renewal.
What did Jesus mean by "this mountain" being cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21)?
On the fulfilled reading, Jesus spoke near Jerusalem, right after cursing the fig tree. "This mountain" may point to the temple mount and its coming removal.

After the fig tree withered, Jesus told his disciples that faith could say to "this mountain", "be taken up and cast into the sea" (Matthew 21:21; Mark 11:23). He spoke on the road to Jerusalem, near the temple mount. On the fulfilled reading, the setting matters. The fig tree pictured the fruitless temple. "This mountain" may picture the temple order that would be removed. In prophecy, the sea often stands for the nations (Isaiah 17:12; Revelation 17:15). Read this way, the old centre of worship would be thrown down, and the gospel would go to the nations. Jesus soon spoke of the temple's fall from the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:1-3). This links the fig tree, the mountain and Zechariah 14.
Mark 11:20-23: the withered fig tree and "this mountain" in one scene.
Revelation 8:8: "a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea" (KJV).

Most interpreters read Matthew 21:21 as a general saying about the power of faith and prayer. Some scholars agree that the temple mount may be in view. Futurists generally do not link it with Zechariah 14.
What does the splitting of the Mount of Olives mean, on the fulfilled reading?
It pictures the breaking down of the barrier between Jew and Gentile. With the old Jerusalem order removed, the way was open for all nations to come to God.

Zechariah 14:4 says the mountain will split from east to west, making a great valley. Some older commentators read this as a picture. The Puritan commentator Matthew Henry said the mountains around Jerusalem stood like a fence between the city and the nations. By Jerusalem's destruction this fence would be opened. The church would then be open to Gentiles, who were made one with the Jews (Ephesians 2:14). Tertullian also linked Zechariah 14:4 to Jesus going out to the Mount of Olives at night (Luke 21:37). On the fulfilled reading, the new valley is a way of escape and of access (Zechariah 14:5). Read this way, Christ's work broke down the dividing wall and made one new people.
Ephesians 2:14: Christ "hath broken down the middle wall of partition" (KJV).
Zechariah 14:5: the people flee through the new valley, a picture of escape.

Futurists read the valley as a real escape route for the Jewish remnant in a future attack. They point to the specific geography. Some amillennialists see a picture of salvation at the last judgment. Many commentators admit the passage is hard and hold their reading with caution.
Does "the LORD will be king over all the earth" (Zechariah 14:9) require an earthly millennium?
The fulfilled reading says no. The Psalms already call God king over all the earth, and the New Testament says Christ now reigns at God's right hand.

Zechariah 14:9 says the LORD will be king over all the earth. In that day there will be one LORD and his name one. Premillennialists see this as Christ's reign after his return. The fulfilled reading notes that the chapter never mentions a thousand years. It also notes that the same language appears where no millennium is in view. "The LORD Most High is ... a great King over all the earth" (Psalms 47:2). On this reading, the New Testament places Christ's kingship now. He is seated at God's right hand (Acts 2:33-36). He has all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). He is "ruler of the kings of the earth" (Revelation 1:5). Read this way, Zechariah 14:9 describes the worldwide reign that began after his ascension.
